p: There were a couple others, so there was protected time off, which was 5 lines according to OMB. Um, I'm trying to think if we missed it. I think that was the only one we missed.
Yeah, these are not your estimates, these are OMB's estimates, right?
I think we worked with OMB on them.
That's correct, that’s part of the hearing and, um, and final aging process, um, these are submitted on the Council's website.

Right and then, uh, I wanna talk about funding that you use to fund community-based organizations who are really doing the good work in the city, talking to immigrant communities, making sure that people understand what the laws are. Can you tell us right now how much funding is available for educating street vendors on their rights and responsibilities?
Let's see.
That you, you allocate directly from, from your agency?
I don't know-

I think that would, that would, that bucket of work would fall into, uh, I believe SBS. Um, uh, they- they have the new division of street vendor support, right? Um, uh, which I, um, that's one piece for that. Um, but we're working closely with SBS and, and Health and, and DSNY to make sure that the city's efforts around street vending are coordinated.

And so, but so, to sound clear, while you're— you have responsibilities to oversee this law, at this point there's no resources going from your agency to help street vendors understand the law, be educated on law through nonprofit organizations who are working with street vendors?

Well, so the street vendor expansion piece, that- that takes effect in January. We've already begun conversations with stakeholders, including Street Vendor Project, about implementation of that law. That includes outreach, for example, on potential waitlists that are gonna be going out. Um,

we anticipate also, um, uh, developing outreach notices and materials for that. But, uh, but I think it's gonna be an all-hands-on-deck action for this. Uh, could include SBS, Office of Mass Engagement. We need to hit the streets. We need to reach people where they are, um, uh, to make sure that people take advantage of this.

Yeah, I understand. Uh, yeah, I appreciate the work that the agency is doing, but also we, you know, have a dedicated group of nonprofits who might need additional resources to collaborate with you. I'm wondering what resources have been set aside in this proposed budget to provide the support that those nonprofits need to help educate the- the community?

I think, I think the money would go through SBS and not through us. We've requested, uh, resources for implementation of the licensing, uh, phase. Uh, SBS is, I think, b-but, by the Council's legislation is, is designed now to provide the support. Um, whether that's, uh, OTPS for partners, I, I'm not sure. Uh, certainly I think they've also received resources, um, for, for PS,

but, you know, I would really defer to them on this, on this question.

I have— and so -on delivery workers, you know, obviously I'm wondering, obviously there are nonprofits who are collaborating with delivery workers, making sure they understand what the rules are of compliance. I'm wondering what resources, uh, you have that fund those nonprofits to do the kind of community education we think is necessary to educate the workers.

I think, um, uh, we— our contracts relate to financial empowerment providers. We offer 2 particular programs, or I should say now it's- it's 3 particular programs, um, uh, um, in our budget. Um, that's, uh, financial empowerment centers, about $4.7 million, free tax prep, also about the same amount and, um, we also have a new initiative related to financial literacy for youth. Um, but those are where our contracts are. Um, uh, I know there are other contracts that the city that provide legal services to workers. I believe those are with HRA. Um, uh, that is certainly very important. I think we, we have all long— we have long thought that, uh, um, organizations like Legal

Aid Society, for example, play an important role in supporting our worker groups. Um, but yeah, that's how our contracts are focused on financial empowerment.

And I would just add very briefly, Chair, um, true. Uh, it is also the case, of course, that we work very closely with WJP and other champions for worker justice, um, who not only, uh, who refer a lot of cases to us, who, who do outreach to workers about the laws. I don't think we are funding them directly in any way, uh, but they've certainly been a critical partner to the successful enforcement of these laws.

Yeah, I, I do appreciate that. I know how important these nonprofit partners are. I just would also add that I know how important it is for them to have resources to be able to, to educate and help, uh, make people understand that these laws exist and to get into communities, especially in limited English proficient communities. These community-based organizations are really a critical part of our city infrastructure. Uh, and I just would hope that we would, as we move forward in this process, the Administration would consider what

resources might be necessary to ensure that th-that we can do this successfully as well in the agency, but also out in the community at large.
Certainly, certainly.

Um, I know, uh, Council Member Banks, um, was trying to Zoom in, and because of some quorum issues, he can't ask questions. So I've been empowered to ask questions on his behalf. Um, so, uh, on small business support, in his district has a high concentration of small immigrant-owned and legacy businesses. What resources in the Preliminary Budget are dedicated to helping those businesses comply with DCWP regulations without over-penalizing, particularly for older business owners who may need additional support navigating compliance requirements?

Yeah, we- we do quite a- a bit on this, Chair. Uh, we do educational events with business-focused stakeholders. We work with BIDs. I've met with BIDs, Chambers of Commerce. Uh, we've already, I think, been in talks with the consumable planning events. We do business education days. We conducted 17 in 2025, where we connected with over 1,000 businesses across the 5 boroughs. Um, we are

aggressive on social media, newsletters, direct mailings to educate businesses. We're very proud of our VIP inspections, which I would love to do with, with any one of you, with, for new licensees to receive an educational inspection, um, from an inspector so that they know what the expectations are. Uh, we, you know, I, I can't underscore it enough. We want small businesses to thrive. We are not out there trying to play gotcha. We have a job to do, but in the first instance, we would love for small businesses to understand their obligations, comply, and if we can be better partners, we certainly will.
Thank you.

I'm fortunate to, to, to do some of these VIP and business education days with Council Member Banks. Um, they're great. They're one-on-one moments for us to interact with the small business community and just to echo the Commissioner again, like, we would love to do that with anybody here at the dais today.
I'm sure all of us will be happy to take out— take you up on that offer. I know, uh-
When it's a little warmer, maybe.

Yeah, it's fine out there. Um, ah, so, you know, I think this is— there's a particular population. I think Council Member Banks is talking about kind of older, uh, business owners. I'm wondering if you're doing anything that's targeting that population, because if you've been in business in a neighborhood for 30, 40, 50 years, and you've been doing what you've been doing and it's been successful, you may not spend a lot of time thinking through what the changing laws are, how you keep up. Like, is there any kind of targeted outreach to that population?

Yeah, I know, I think that's right. I mean, one of the very exciting things about this new Administration is all the, you know, great outreach we're doing through, you know, TikTok and Instagram and online. But the reality is, for a lot of small business owners, it's better to show up in person and I think especially for older small business owners, it's better to show up at their

door, again, not to conduct an inspection in the traditional sense, but in the case of our VIP inspections to educate people. So I think the best thing we can do for older small business owners really is showing up. Um, an email might not work. TikTok video probably isn't gonna work, but showing up with real people saying, maybe a Council Member too, we're here to support you. We're here to make sure you understand this is the sign, you know, you need to post. Uh, that's something we love to do. Uh, and I think for older business owners especially, I think that is where you get the most responsiveness.

So I feel like this goes back to that resource conversation. It sounds like we- we'd love to do this more and maybe this requires some additional resources to be able to do a more robust engagement with older businesses. But I don't want to speak for Council Member Banks on that, but it sounds like it's really great that we're doing it and the more we can do, the better it is to prevent bad things from happening to good businesses.
That's a very good way of putting it, Chair.
Uh, can the Department provide data on consumer complaints regarding— originating from the 42nd Council District and how those complaints are being prioritized and resolved?
What was the last thing you said? I'm sorry.
From his district, the 42nd Council District. He would like a summary of complaints from his district.
I don't have those available at hand, but we- we can get that data. I have the total number of complaints, which is about $30,000 last year, mostly-
For the city.
Yeah, I mean, Council Member Banks said $30,000.
Yeah, a very complaining district. Now, $30,000 for the city, uh, we can get him specific information.
Yeah, I'm sure other people would love to have it too.
We're happy to send to them.
Yeah, I would love to share that as well.

And I hope all of you know, I imagine, there really are no wrong doors with respect to your constituents if they have complaints. You can call us, you can write us a letter, you can— they call 311, you go through- The best system for us internally is to go to nyc.gov/consumers or nyc.gov/dcwp and file a complaint but any way we get it, we'll process it and we'll try to mediate it and get people their money back.

Great uh, so Council Member Banks introduced, uh, Intro 1231 of 2025 last session, requires tax preparers to provide consumers with clear itemized statements on charges and fees, but before and after services provided. Um, and then so it was driven by, uh, people felt like they didn't get transparency in pricing on, on that. Are there other industries similar to tax preparation where fee transparency remains a concern for DCWP?

Uh, I'd be hard-pressed to identify industries where fee transparency is not a concern, uh, for DCWP. I think tax is especially problematic. In- in a previous life, I- I sued

TurboTax and H&R. It's not just small-time scammers on the corner. These are large publicly traded companies ripping off low-income taxpayers who should be entitled to free tax prep, are told they're gonna get free tax prep, and then 3 hours into the process learn they have to pay a $75 fee. And we know that this is happening from publicly traded multinational companies all the way down to corner stores that are ripping people off. So we- we're doing a sweep of inspections around free tax prep, but there are other industries, and unfortunately they are industries that prey on the people who are already the most vulnerable. We've done a sweep recently of employment agencies. These are folks who are searching for jobs who are being charged exorbitant amounts for services they can do for free. Uh, we've done a sweep of, uh, er, grocery stores to make sure people aren't getting ripped off there. We are really looking— used car dealers, where we've seen a lot of problems. We've been sending inspectors all all over the city. Um, so there are unfortunately a lot of industries that are, uh, tricking people about prices and fees, and that is

why we're proud to lead and be implementing the Mayor's efforts to crack down on junk fees marketwide.

Yeah, and I do just want to underscore, um, the reference to employment agencies. We've brought several cases over the last year about illegal advance fees being charged by, uh, employment agencies. Definitely been a point of focus for our work, um, very recently.

Thank you and then many parts of this district, residents and workers are simply not aware of the protections available to them. Uh, he's asking about budgets for community outreach, language access, education campaigns for consumers and business owners.

Um, I could say— just, sorry, I'm thinking about the order of this. Um, our community affairs team is, uh, 6 people strong. Um, uh, they with— between themselves, they cover 7 to 8 languages. Um, uh, er, additionally, we have OTPS available to produce materials, and oftentimes our materials are- are more than 11 languages that the city requires.

Um, I would also note too that we get a lot of support from our- our team across the agency. You know, we have about 400, uh, staff members on our team, uh, but they cover over 40 languages. Uh, nearly 50% of our agency speaks a language other than English. Um, uh, and so I think it's— it really helps us to be very accessible to all diverse language communities.
Yeah, I know Council Member Banks is interested in having more on-the-ground, um, walkthroughs in his district, so I would ask if you had committed to- to doing those?
Yeah, absolutely, we'd love to.

Great, so you help them with the business owners' education, enforcement issues. And, uh, next, he wanted to make sure— he's got a lot of street vendors in his district, um, and he wants to know if there's, ah, funding available to do outreach.
Asked an answer-

Education. I feel like I just heard this, that we would love more funding for outreach and education for street vendors, um, and

partnerships. He mentioned Street Vendor Project, support those efforts.
Indeed, yes, we- we support those efforts.

Okay, thank you. I, I wanna talk to you about finally the student loans. Um, you own partnership with Summer appears to deliver some results. He wants to know kind of, er, what data you have around Summer. Is it working? Is it not? How many people are they seeing? What are the impacts? You know, they've had a decent, ah, foot- financial footprint. I think it's $3 million a quarter, $12 million for this past fiscal year.

Yeah, that's right. Well, we know that, uh, we estimate that 1.4 New Yorkers are struggling with student loan debt and we serve them in a number of ways. As you referenced, we have a program with Summer, uh, uh, that has served, uh, I believe thousands of New Yorkers have created accounts, uh, including many city employees. We do financial— our financial empowerment centers offer student loan counseling services. More than 9,000 people used our financial empowerment

centers last year. A couple hundred of them used student loan services. We do a lot of outreach and education around student loan services. We do referrals to EDCAP too, and we, uh, we don't fund them directly, but we will work with EDCAP closely. And we appreciate, uh, Intro 177, your legislation Chair, um, because I, I do think, given what is happening in Washington and the prospect of widespread defaults, uh, student loan defaults for New Yorkers, we really do have to make sure these efforts are coordinated and integrated to reach as many New Yorkers as we can.
Thank you. Um, I'm gonna go start round 2, and Shirley, you can go first.

Thank you, Chair. Uh, I do have a question about revenue raising, and, um, have you— you know, DCWP, uh, your enforcement programs can, uh, raise revenue through fees and fines collected from bad actors, and, um, you know, has, has there been any analysis done about the long-term revenue raising impacts, uh, of shorter-term investments in, in the DCWP staff budget?

Uh, good questions, and I'll do my best and then turn things over to my colleagues as needed. You know, our goal is never fines and fees as such. Our goal is a more fair economy, but often the way you do that is through fines and fees. You have to deter- you have to punish wrong behavior, you have to deter it for others. In 2025, we collected $15.8 million in fines and penalties. It's about the same as in 2024. Um, in terms of projection going forward, um, it is the case that enforcement, our- our enforcement of key worker protection laws can return millions of dollars, not only to workers and consumers, but also to the city treasury. Um, my understanding is that our revenue targets for, I believe, the just for our worker protection efforts are about $300,000. We regularly exceed that by at least an order of magnitude. Um, so I think we really are overperforming when it comes— again, the goal is not revenue, the goal is justice for our workers, but the reality is that does lead to penalties that benefit the city treasury, uh, far in excess of what OMB has targeted for us.
Thank you.
Thank you. Um, so I have a couple more questions if that's okay with you.

Of course. So I want to figure out if we can break down what's, what's the budget for consumer protection and what's being budgeted for worker protection, so we can figure out where the balance is. I, I hear the- the $387 is your total lines, and I hear that you're having 20 to 25 lawyers, which is a big difference between 20 and 25, and 15 to 20 lawyers. So I'm wondering, do they overlap, or do they— like, how does this break down? Are people specialized in doing this work? You know, are the lawyers specialized? Or, you know, I know we talked a little bit about the inspectors having some specialization.

Yeah, I, I can give you a bit of an overview and then my colleagues will jump in with some more details. So we do our consumer protect— we specialize basically in terms of our outward enforcement work. We basically have two buckets. We have work protection, we have consumer protection.

Um, Worker Protection sits under Liz's team at the Office of Labor Policy and Standards. Consumer Protection sits under Mike's team at General Counsel. Um, hmm, the headcount for General Counsel is at 83 active, but again, that's over-inclusive in some ways because that's not just the lawyers bringing enforcement cases. That includes legal counsel.

Yeah, I think, you know, we took— we talked about this like a little bit earlier, um, that we have not a bunch of the non-lawyer units of the agency are within the General Counsel Division. So that's when we drilled down down before, and about like the 20 to 25 attorneys that work on consumer protection work. So just to serve— get— they're, they're generalists. Um, they come in, they don't—
They do anything. They do any kind of case. So they— in the consumer protection lane, they do any kind of case.

Yeah, they may get a case against a used car dealership, they may get a case against a debt collector. Now, naturally, like in any workplace, like in any regulatory enforcement agency,

you organically develop expert expertise and become a subject matter expert. So the people who do, who do well and, you know, uh, bring excellent, like, used car cases, they will naturally, um, have more used car cases. They developed an expertise, and that's, like, organically happens but we don't necessarily bring in attorneys with specializations in the many, many, many industries that fall in within DCWP's jurisdiction.

I'll also just add briefly that the- the majority of our OTPS budget is essentially, the vast majority is essentially pass-through. So our total OTPS budget for FY '27 based on the JAM plan is $36.9 million. Uh, $12.7 million of that is through Kids Rise. That's straight pass-through. We don't administer it. Uh, $7.6 million goes through our youth empower— excuse me, through our financial youth— excuse me, through our financial counseling programs, including youth financial empowerment. Um, $5 million goes to nonprofits that do free tax prep, $4.1 million for our beautiful building down the street, um, beautiful offices and then our remaining OTPS budget to invest in the kind of software, for example, we need to do worker

protection cases, tools Mike's team— Mike's team needs to investigate consumer protection cases. That's all under $7 million.

Thank you, very helpful. Uh, we noticed that the revenue projections for Fiscal Year 2027 are $1.3 mill- million dollars lower than the Fiscal, uh, in 2026. Is there a reason why, uh, those revenue, uh, expectations are lower?

I, I think, um, I think we'd have to circle back with- with OMB about those revenue projections they have for us but to the Commissioner's point earlier, we, we frequently exceed our- our revenue targets.
Just a clarifying question on that. Is that from the PMMR?
Yeah.
Okay.
It'd be great to know why they're lower and whose projections are lower, based on— it sounds like you're doing additional enforcement and we would expect that, that not to be lower.
Yeah, we're, we're bringing more than $1 million in. Yeah.
Great.
Oh, already in 2026, I believe.

Can I ask you about the, the current vacancies you mentioned earlier? You had 60-odd vacancies and is your expectation that you're filling those vacancies before the end of the fiscal year or are those vacancies remaining vacant through June 30th?
Well, do you want to talk about the vacancies and the- the challenges posed?

Yes. So, I mean, I think as we mentioned earlier, currently we're in a 2-for-1 hiring. Um, uh, we, we work, you know, we've submitted, uh, um, candidates for hiring and we work through OMB on, on getting those, um, uh, fulfilled. Um, if I could walk through the vacancies, I'd say that, uh, 20 of those vacancies are in our, uh, Department of Health licensing, uh, unit. Um, the next highest—
Which we don't control.

Which we don't control. Ah, that's a good point. That's what I was trying to get to. I'm sorry. Uh, the, the highest, the highest vacancies are in the Department of Health. We

coordinate with Department of Health on those hirings, and we- we work at the direction to get those in. Um, I think a problem is that those vacancies end up being a part of our overall vacancy reduction target. Um, so it does create difficulties in terms of how much the agency needs to, uh, meet for a project to eliminate the gap. Um, but for the most part, overall, like, our vacancy rate is, um, for our, for our DCP divisions is fairly low.

And if I could just underscore a point my colleague alluded to, you know, there are, I understand, 20 vacancies right now for DOHMH. We-we cannot close those vacancies. So when we get a vacancy reduction target that includes DOHMH lines in the target, that, um, that disproportionately falls on consumer and worker protection because those 20 vacancies from DOHMH are untouchable.
Okay, so of the 40-odd other vacancies, are you planning to try to fill those before the end of the Fiscal Year?
100%. We wanna fill those, but we're— but we will— we need to make sure that those conversations with OMB are successful.
So is it like, you know, so I'm clear, you've gone to OMB asking them for the ability to hire and they've said yes on the 2-to-1 and then you're posted and looking for applicants?
So, um, I'm not sure. We are, we are looking to hire. We- we interview, we make sure we, we do our step of the process to hire people, bring people in.
Right.
Those hires are still subject to the 2-for-1 rule.

Right and so, and then you've gone to OMB with actual names on the 2-for-1 rule saying, hey, we have these 10 people for these 20 lines. That we wanna hire and we wanna do it now. Has that happened or are you just in some other process? You've lost people. That's why you have vacancies, right?

I think it's, ah, er, ah, hmm, mhm, like, you know, I mean, all over the lifecycle of the hiring process. I'd say for virtually every one of the vacancies, we have posted it across all the divisions in DCWP and there are ones where we

have interviewed and that we have made a conditional offer to, and we're waiting for OMB clearance. There are ones where we are engaging in active interviewing, and there are ones where we have just recently posted the lines.
Okay, so is your expectation that we— you're trying to, uh, hire some of those lines between now and the end of the Fiscal Year?

Yeah, I think a great example of this, of this life cycle of vacancies is we just received 9 new lines in the Preliminary Budget. Those are, you know, those are going up, those postings, they have gone up.
Right.
And so that's a vacancy, for example, that's in the early steps of, —us actively working to hire.

Right, so we move as quickly as possible to interview people, select a candidate, get an accepted offer, and then at— that's the point at which it goes to OMB for approval to actually onboard the person. Um, so we're able to move very

quickly up until that point where we have someone sign— waiting for permission to onboard.
So do you have people waiting for OMB approval?
We do.
And how many lines is that?
I don't think we have that number with us. We do have some. I just want to add to—
Could you get us that number?
Sure, yeah.
Thank you.

Just, uh, to add to the, uh, complexity, that's the rich tapestry of hiring in New York City. Um, a lot of times what we're talking about are the non-competitive lines, like for the lawyers, but there are also obviously competitive civil service titles where you have to call from a pool. So there's a whole different process for sort of teeing up having a pool call that's unnecessarily complex and goes beyond the scope of, uh, what we can talk about today. But just to say there, we are attempting through whatever the necessary route is

for hiring for individual positions, we are trying to hire for those positions.
It'd be great to know how many of those are sitting at OMB and just waiting for decisions. That would be great to know.
Sure.
Is your expectation, Commissioner, that, um, with additional hiring you could provide additional resources to the city because the - the the fees and fines that may be collected?
Absolutely, to say nothing of millions of dollars for consumers and workers in money they are owed.
Is it, is it your expectation that without additional hires, New Yorkers will not be able to collect those millions of dollars in fees and fines?

It will mean a substantial reduction in both the amount of back pay and compensation we can get for workers, compensation we can get for consumers, and, and, uh, effective enforcement of the laws to protect marketplaces. So yes.
And so besides resources, are there additional tools you think at this point that the- the agency needs to be able to advance your overall goal of protecting consumers and workers?

I think, you know, one thing that we are really striving to do is get the word out to the people of New York that if they're being cheated, whether it's on the job or at the grocery store or wherever it may be, to come to DCWP. We are getting- we’ve already seen a pretty significant increase in the number of complaints in 2026. I think that's because of the great uplift we've had from members of the Council, from the Mayor about the important work we do. So I do want more consumers and workers, more New Yorkers coming in the door to tell us about what's happening. Of course, our ability to actually respond to those complaints will depend on resources. I can also tell you particularly in, in particular, you know, part of that is of course people, but part of it also is systems, you know, we just did a hotel junk fee rule. We don't have economists internally who can estimate how much that's gonna save, which I think is important for people to know. A data

scientist who can look at, uh, one of Liz's big cases and figure out, you know, it can be hard to figure out exactly how much a worker was underpaid across many years. Uh, we need really good data scientists to do that. So it's not just about, no offense, the lawyers. It's, it's, it's also about the data scientists and economists who— to support our work.
Yeah, I mean, speaking of—
No offense to you either—

All the lawyers in the room, I sense we need a lot more support for your agency in a lot of different ways to be doing that. Can we talk about the- the student loan issue? Um, can you talk about the contracts this company Summer has, what data information you have from them, how successful can we see they are so far, and when their contract expires?

Um, I wanna— for some of those more specific questions, I'm gonna defer to Carlos. My understanding is that they contract with Summer was entered into in 2025. Um, the, uh, er, I, I, do you wanna get into sort of the budgeting, how it's being budgeted, Carlos?
Uh, maybe we— how many people it's serving, you know-
We -we have that information. I don't know if we can get it to you.

I don't know if we have that information with us right now. I think Summer started last year in May as a pilot program for, for employees. The, the, the city employees, I should say. The pilot was expanded in August, um, significantly. Um, it's been— and it's also, um, significant— expanded simply to residents across the city. I'm sorry. Um, I think since that time in August, we've been evaluating how it's been working out for workers. I mean, for, for city workers and for residents. Um, it's something that, um, uh, we're looking into it. We- we also recently put up an ad campaign around our financial empowerment center services. Including, uh, our nyc.gov/studentloans, uh, that links to Summer too, uh, to make sure that we're connecting New Yorkers with, um, uh, these services. Um, I, I think we have taken a two-pronged approach, both in my, uh, our website, but also our financial

empowerment centers, to be able to provide New Yorkers with student loan debt assistance.

And so with Summer doing— they mentioned we were expanding the work in the hospitals for financial empowerment, doing Uh, find tax prep in hospitals and community-based organizations. Is Summer doing that on the ground as well?
No, those are community partners doing that.
And so Summer is just uh, people have to go to Summer, or is it online?
It's an, it's an online portal that people can go to.

Okay, I think I would love some more details about how many people are going through that portal, how many people are getting served, what the benefits of that portal are, knowing that we have a very be, um, you know, a lot of seniors and immigrants maybe not have access to that portal, not know how to use it, and, you know, questions of veracity of putting information in a portal.

Yeah, and I will just say, yes, so there is that portal, and I, I think we could get you those numbers, but we'll confirm. Um, I will also say, and I really want to stress this to people, our financial empowerment centers provide student loan counseling. It's not on a website. It's not a phone call. It is in person. Personalized people can come in with their manila folders full of papers and our financial counselors will help them sort them out and set them straight. I don't mean set them straight, but get them on a path to financial well-being.
So just to— just so I understand it, the additional, uh, funding for Summer, what additive value does it have in addition to what you're already doing then?

Well, I understand that Summer offers, uh, I believe they specialize in public service loan forgiveness and income-driven repayment. I believe they also do quality checks when people submit applications. Um, but it is also the case that our financial empowerment centers do provide this service in person, um, to New Yorkers who- who seek it out and we have great partners there.

It's a program that we're in the midst of evaluating, and I think we're gonna come to a decision about. Um, uh, what metrics— and we can share this with Council too, um, but what, what metrics, um, um, we can identify to help us make our decision about the longevity of the program.

I'd appreciate that. Some, you know, ongoing conversations around it. So on tobacco enforcement, we've seen a real reduction in tobacco enforcement. I'm wondering why that's happening. Obviously tobacco is a problem, and, you know, we in my district, we've seen a lot of uh, illegal sales of tobacco. We've had the Sheriff's Department go out numerous times to numerous locations, and I'm just wondering, what do you— what do you account for the reduction in that kind of tobacco enforcement?

I'm gonna let, um, Mike jump in in a minute, but my understanding is that there was significant efforts last year with the Sheriff to shut down a lot of illegal smoke shops, which has, I think— so I think there was an unusual spike last year, which might explain the reduction this year. But Mike, why don't you add to that?
